title: Solving wave propagation problems via geometric quantum state preparation on dispersion manifolds
authors: Yakov Solomons, Lee Peleg, Netanel Barel, Jonathan Nemirovsky, Amit Ben-Kish, Yotam Shapira
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for solving partial differential equations through a linear-system formulation, focusing on wave propagation problems described by the discretized Helmholtz equation in frequency domain. Although quantum linear-system solvers offer exponential compression of the system degrees of freedom, their runtime complexity is generally governed by the condition number of the discretized operator. Exploiting the analytic structure of the differential operator can provide an alternative to explicit matrix inversion, as illustrated for the screened Poisson equation through an explicit quantum circuit. For the Helmholtz equation, however, the inverse operator becomes singular on the dispersion surface $k^2=ω^2/c^2$, rendering direct Fourier-space state-preparation methods exponentially inefficient. We address this challenge by directly preparing quantum states supported on the resonant manifold and encoding source locations through Fourier phases. The resulting algorithm eliminates the exponentially large overhead associated with post-selection on the resonant manifold, yielding a success probability that depends linearly on the number of sources and is independent of the computational domain size. More generally, our approach applies to hyperbolic differential equations whose Fourier-space solutions possess singular support on dispersion manifolds, recasting their solution as a problem of geometric quantum state preparation.
summary: This paper presents a quantum algorithm to solve wave propagation problems by bypassing the limitations of standard quantum linear system solvers. Instead of inverting the full operator, the authors directly prepare quantum states supported on the resonant manifold defined by the wave equation's dispersion relation. This novel geometric approach removes exponential overhead, making the computation feasible regardless of the physical domain size.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of solving wave propagation partial differential equations (PDEs) using quantum algorithms, specifically overcoming the exponential inefficiency encountered when dealing with singular operators.
main_result: By developing a method of geometric quantum state preparation directly on the resonant manifold, the authors eliminate the exponential overhead associated with post-selection, leading to a success probability independent of the computational domain size.
method: The approach reformulates the problem from inverting the full discretized operator to preparing a quantum state whose support is restricted to the known resonant manifold, utilizing quantum comparators and arithmetic circuits.
model_or_system: The model is wave propagation, exemplified by the Helmholtz equation, which is discretized into a linear system. The core difficulty arises from the singularity of the inverse operator on the dispersion surface $k^2 = \omega^2/c^2$.
key_observables: Success probability ($P_{	ext{succ}}$) for state preparation, which is shown to scale favorably with the number of sources and independently of domain size.
important_parameters: The condition number $\kappa(A)$ of the discretized operator, the resonant manifold itself, and the source location encoding via Fourier phases.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the hyperbolic PDE solutions possess singular support on lower-dimensional dispersion manifolds, allowing for geometric state preparation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuits for preparing states corresponding to geometric shapes, such as the Midpoint (Bresenham) circle algorithm and a finite-width resonant ring in momentum space.
paper_structure: The paper first contrasts standard Quantum Linear System Solvers (QLSS) with the wave equation's singular structure. It then introduces the novel geometric state preparation technique, detailing the quantum circuits required to construct states supported only on the resonant manifold, culminating in the derivation of the size-independent success probability.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete quantum algorithmic pathway for solving fundamental PDEs in physics (like wave equations) that are notoriously difficult for standard quantum linear solvers due to spectral singularities.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Quantum implementation of the inverse operator for the screened Poisson equation in Fourier space. The Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) maps the state to the momentum basis, where the differential operator becomes diagonal, this corresponds to the U operation in the main text . In this basis, inversion reduces to evaluating the scalar function q(k) = 1/(k2 +C), (16). This value is computed by quantum arithmetic and then encoded into an auxiliary qubit amplitude through a controlled rotation, (17), producing the state q(k) |0⟩+ p

FIG. 2. Illustration of the (a) real and (b) imaginary parts of Eq. (20), corresponding to the principal-value and delta- function contributions, respectively. The computation is per- formed on a discretized 64 × 64 grid over a square domain of side length L = 16λ, where λ denotes the wavelength. As seen, both terms are concentrated around the dispersion sur- face k2 = ω2/c2 = 2π/λ. Here, ϵ = 3∆kω/c

FIG. 3. Quantum circuit for the geometric quantum state preparation algorithm. The momentum registers are first initialized in the resonant state by the state-preparation procedure described in Appendix A. The source-dependent phase encoding, highlighted by the dashed box, is then implemented by controlled phase gates that apply the phases ei(kxxj+kyyj). Finally, after unpreparing the source register and post-selecting it onto |0⟩⊗m, inverse quantum Fourier transform (iQFT) is applied to the momentum registers, yielding the solution state |u(x, y)⟩.

FIG. 4. Accuracy of the resonant-ring approximation. (a) Total overlap error, 1 −|⟨uC|uQ⟩|, between the normalized classical solution |uC⟩and the state |uQ⟩obtained from the resonant-ring approximation, as a function of the ring width, computed on a 64 × 64 spatial grid. The highlighted point corresponds to the simulation of Fig. 6. (b) Error in the real and imaginary parts of the solution, corresponding to the real (principal-value) and imaginary (delta-function) parts of q(k), respectively.

FIG. 5. Minimum resonant-ring width required to achieve target approximation errors of 0.05 and 0.01 as a function of the computational domain size. The slight increase for the smallest domains is due to the coarse Fourier discretization. At higher resolution, the required ring width approaches a constant value, indicating independence from the domain size.
